articles.title: Joshua Wong, face of Hong Kong's pro-democracy protests, jailed for 10 years
articles.summary: Wong, 30, is among hundreds of Hongkongers detained under the controversial national security law.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Hong Kong pro-democracy advocate Joshua Wong jailed for 10 years By Abel U ,  BBC Chinese ,  Reporting from Hong Kong   and   Kelly Ng 
- Published 5 November 2026 
Joshua Wong, once the face of Hong Kong's democracy movement, has been sentenced to 10 years in jail for colluding with foreign forces under the city's sweeping national security law. 
Wong is among hundreds of campaigners and ordinary Hongkongers arrested under the law, which was imposed in 2020 following explosive pro-democracy protests against Beijing's growing control. 
Critics say the far-reaching law has silenced dissent, but authorities argue that it is needed to maintain stability and deny it has weakened the city's cherished autonomy. 
Having already spent the last six years in jail, Wong, who was due to be freed in January, will now spend another decade behind bars. 
- 
Silenced and erased, Hong Kong's decade of protest is now a defiant memory 
- Published 30 November 2024 
- 
What a defiant mogul's trial says about Hong Kong 
- Published 18 December 2023 
Wong, who turned 30 last month, has already been imprisoned multiple times for his activism which started when he was in his early teens. 
On Thursday, he arrived in court wearing a dark blue long-sleeved shirt, khaki trousers and black-rimmed glasses. He looked slimmer compared to his previous public appearances. 
He nodded in greeting towards members of the packed public gallery, and took notes intermittently as the judge read out the reasons for his sentencing. 
A crowd had gathered outside the court, with dozens of Hongkongers having queued for hours hoping to get a seat in the public gallery. There was also a heavy police presence. 
Wong is already serving time for subversion and was due to be freed early next year when he was handed the latest charges, to which he pleaded guilty in September. 
Two months and two days of the 10-year term will be served concurrently with his ongoing sentence, the judge said on Thursday. 
Prosecutors said Wong had conspired with other campaigners, including self-exiled activist Nathan Law, to lobby for foreign sanctions and blockades against Beijing. 
These activities took place between July and late November 2020, the court heard. 
Wong and Law had been co-founders of Demosisto, a now defunct pro-democracy political party. 
On Thursday, Hong Kong's chief executive John Lee said Wong and Law were "among the primary culprits responsible for undermining Hong Kong's prosperity and stability". 
Their actions "not only severely undermined national sovereignty, security, and development interests, but also directly prejudiced the well-being of the general public and the stability of society," Lee said in a statement issued after the ruling. 
Beijing's foreign ministry said China "firmly supports [Hong Kong] in safeguarding national security in accordance with the law". It also called on "relevant parties" to "earnestly respect China's sovereignty and Hong Kong's legal system". 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Wong's (left) activism started when he was just 14 
Wong's friend and fellow activist Frances Hui, now based in the US, said she was "heartbroken" and "outraged" by the verdict. 
"Today's sentencing is not just about Joshua. It is part of a broader political crackdown that seeks to rewrite a chapter of Hong Kong's history and erase the contributions of an entire generation who believed they could shape the future of their city," she told the BBC. 
The UK said the sentencing was "a clear example of how the National Security Law is being used to target individuals for political expression and participation". In a statement shared with the BBC, a UK government spokesperson called for "an immediate end to all unjust prosecutions" of individuals charged under the NSL. 
According to the US consulate in Hong Kong, the sentencing showed Beijing "will go to extraordinary lengths to silence those who advocate for fundamental freedoms" in the Chinese territory. 
Human Rights Watch described the sentence as "cruel and unjust". 
"To keep Hong Kong society subdued, and to reduce the chance of an international outcry, the Hong Kong government appears to have adopted the tactic of stacking charges against influential pro-democracy leaders," said its Asia director Elaine Pearson. 
The harshest sentence under the controversial national security law (NSL) thus far has been handed to 78-year-old former media tycoon Jimmy Lai, who was jailed for 20 years , also after having been found guilty of colluding with foreign forces. 
Who is Joshua Wong? 
Born to IT professional Roger and homemaker Grace in October 1996, Wong was diagnosed with dyslexia as a child, which made him struggle with school. 
However, he was quick to challenge established rules and norms when they didn't make sense. In secondary school, he rallied with his classmates to protest against the high prices of canteen lunches on Facebook. 
In 2011, Wong, then 14, co-founded the pro-democracy student activist group Scholarism, which quickly grew in size and influence. 
The following year, the group rallied more than 100,000 people to protest against Hong Kong's plans to implement mandatory "patriotic education" in schools, forcing the authorities to back down. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
At 30, Wong has already been imprisoned multiple times for his activism 
By 2014, Wong, who was then at the forefront of a civil disobedience movement known as the "Umbrella Movement", had already become one of the most recognisable faces among Hong Kong's pro-democracy activists. 
In 2016, he co-founded Demosisto with Nathan Law and Agnes Chow, activists who are now based overseas. 
But he often expressed discomfort at being labelled a "protest leader". 
"We have a lot of facilitators in this movement and I'm one of them... Instead of having a top-down command, we now have a bottom-up command hub," Wong told The Financial Times in November 2019. 
Demosisto disbanded in 2020, the year Beijing introduced the NSL in Hong Kong. 
Law left for the UK and continued his advocacy abroad, while Wong stayed on in Hong Kong and tried to run for a seat in its legislature – but was barred, with authorities citing his opposition to the NSL as one of the reasons. 
Meanwhile, the court cases against Wong were stacking up. 
On 23 November 2020, he pleaded guilty to several charges related to his involvement in protests outside the Hong Kong police headquarters in 2019. 
Then came the NSL charges. While still in prison in February 2021, Wong was among 47 people charged with "conspiracy to commit subversion". The group became known as the Hong Kong 47 and remains the largest prosecution so far under the NSL. 
Wong was still serving his 56-month sentence for the subversion conviction when he was charged with collusion under the NSL last year. 
On 22 November 2020, the day before he pleaded guilty to the protest charges, Wong wrote in a post on Instagram addressed to "the people of Hong Kong": "To be honest, I have never had much faith in Hong Kong's politics, but I have every confidence in the people of Hong Kong. 
"Even as political power now poses a comprehensive challenge to the resilience of our civil society, I believe the people of Hong Kong will, as always, find a way to see things through."

articles.title: Weapon or wine bottle? China disputes reports of artillery shell in Papua New Guinea
articles.summary: Papua New Guinea police had earlier dismissed speculation that the 32kg object was "merely a dummy".
articles.full_text:
Image source, PNG East New Britain Province Facebook page Image caption, 
The 32kg object was found at a construction site in Port Moresby By Kelly Ng 
- Published 4 November 2026 
Chinese authorities have dismissed reports that a suspected China-made artillery shell was found in a commercial shipping container in Papua New Guinea, saying it is a "shell-shaped wine bottle". 
"It poses no danger at all," the Chinese embassy wrote in a Facebook post on Tuesday, drawing sceptical comments. 
Police in Port Moresby arrested four Chinese nationals last Friday after the 32kg object was found at a construction site in the capital city. 
Authorities were looking into whether it was a live device, local reports said then, with police commissioner David Manning describing it as "a very concerning discovery". 
In a report on Wednesday, the Australia Broadcasting Corporation cited unnamed sources identifying the object as an undetonated 130mm Chinese Type 59 Artillery Projectile that contains chemical explosives and a fuse. The BBC has not independently verified this. 
Papua New Guinea police had earlier dismissed speculation that the object was "merely a dummy", local newspaper Post Courier said. 
However, the Chinese embassy said in its statement that it is "virtually impossible" for an illegal military-grade artillery shell to be smuggled out of China to Papua New Guinea. 
"China enforces some of the world's strictest firearm control laws and regulations," it wrote, adding that China is "widely recognised as one of the safest countries globally". 
Some Facebook users appear unconvinced. 
"What sort of wine bottle weighs 32 kilograms?" wrote one of them. 
Another wrote that the object bore no labels indicating that it's a wine bottle.

articles.title: Typhoons batter East Asia as El Niño makes Pacific 'burn with fever'
articles.summary: Even for countries where typhoons are a way of life, the last few months have brought unusually wild weather.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Fishermen return to sea under a crimson sky in August after China's Jiangsu province is hit by Super Typhoon Dolphin By Joel Guinto ,  Reporting from Singapore ,  Kurumi Mori ,  Tokyo correspondent   and   Darren Bett ,  Lead weather presenter 
- Published 4 November 2026 
Wild weather is a way of life for people living along the coast in the Philippines, Taiwan, China and Japan. But the last few months have been extraordinary. 
A wave of intense and, at times, unpredictable storms exacerbated by the El Niño weather pattern has killed dozens, shuttered major airports and wiped out crops and infrastructure across a swathe of East Asia. 
In October, nearly all of Taiwan shut down as a monster storm big enough to engulf the island of 23 million roared towards its north-eastern coast. Equivalent to a category five hurricane, Typhoon Champi's 295km/h (193mph) winds had the power to flatten homes and whip up destructive waves. 
Thankfully it did not make landfall in Taiwan, skirting past the island while dousing it in rain. But it had far-reaching impacts : hundreds of flights were cancelled in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. In the Philippines' Batanes archipelago, seaside highways shut as huge waves crashed onto the shore, and in southern Japan's Okinawa islands, power was cut to 15,000 homes. 
El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon in which warm waters pooling in the eastern Pacific and altered wind patterns drive extreme weather events around the world. 
It happens around every two to seven years, lasting for around a year. This year's El Niño, which the UK Met Office has forecast to be the "strongest in living memory", is likely to last until February or March. 
In June, Japan watched two storms - Typhoon Mekkhala and Severe Tropical Storm Higos - race towards its eastern coast simultaneously, forcing one million people to evacuate. In July, Tropical Storm Narra grazed China's southern coast along Guangxi, submerging villages and displacing tens of thousands. 
Image source, VCG via Getty Images Image caption, 
This riverside park in the south-eastern Chinese city of Nanning was submerged by Tropical Storm Narra 
August brought Super Typhoon Dolphin, which churned across the Pacific for 16 days - before slamming into eastern China, triggering heavy floods and dozens of casualties . 
Later that month Typhoon Saudel made landfall in three south-eastern Chinese cities over one week, shutting transport networks and forcing thousands to evacuate. 
'Burning with fever' 
The Pacific Ocean, heated to record levels by El Niño, is now brimming with typhoon energy, according to the Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) metric which measures the total intensity of a season's storms. This year, the ACE reading for South East and East Asia is forecast to be nearly double the 30-year average. 
El Niño also affects wind patterns and in this case, that means typhoons are tending to form further east than usual. They are also becoming stronger as they remain over warm waters for longer. 
The Pacific can be likened to someone "burning with fever", says Ana Liza Solis, head of climatology at the Philippines' national weather bureau. "It can go into convulsions soon," she said at a press briefing in Manila in September. 
Forecasts suggest the worst may not be over. Last month, sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific - the area monitored by the Japan Meteorological Agency for its El Niño predictions - soared to 4C above normal, the highest since records began in 1949. The previous record - 3.6C - was set in December 1997. 
China's climate agency has warned of sea surface temperatures continuing to rise over the next three months because of the El Niño. 
Despite typhoon season usually peaking around September to October, this is likely to raise concerns across a region that has already been battered by back-to-back storms. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
China has seen back-to-back typhoons as the 2026 El Niño intensifies 
'Very, very scary' simulations 
In August, Typhoon Chan-Hom baffled storm watchers in Japan by crossing the country from east to west, as opposed to the usual south-to-north trajectory. Japan's well-resourced and prepared authorities were able to evacuate people swiftly, but this would be far more challenging in some neighbouring countries. 
To get a better picture of how rising temperatures could amplify the risks, Manila-based climatologist Rafaela Jane Delfino and colleagues simulated the effects of warmer conditions on the Philippines' most recent monster storms, including 2013's Super Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) which killed more than 6,000 people. 
They arrived at what she describes as "very, very scary findings": higher temperatures increased total accumulated rainfall by 26%. It's a devastating prospect in a country where flooding from monsoon rains and some 20 tropical storms per year has emerged as one of the main disaster risks. 
In recent years, floods have paralysed entire cities for days, and tired of the annual ordeal, Filipinos have taken to the streets to protest against corruption which they say is gnawing away at millions of dollars from flood-control projects. 
Delfino, in an article on the University of the Philippines website, insists leaders and officials must gain a better understanding of climate hazards if communities are to be better prepared. 
Figure caption, 
Tide of rubbish blankets Philippines river in August after weeks of monsoon rains 
Preparing for the onslaught 
Countries are bracing for the immediate impact. Japan has urged citizens to stockpile food and essentials for the typhoon season , and to secure outdoor furniture that could become deadly projectiles when typhoon winds hit. China has asked local officials to identify vulnerable areas and is upgrading its warning and monitoring systems. 
The Philippines and its South East Asian neighbours are preparing for disruptions to food production, especially rice, and have increased support for famers, including the provision of fertilisers. 
But what happens in the long term is less clear. The window for governments to act on El Niño is "closing", the United Nations Development Programme in Asia and the Pacific said recently. 
"How severely a community experiences an El Niño is decided years in advance, by where roads and settlements are built, how water is managed, who is covered by social protection and whether public budgets have room to absorb a shock. 
"Every El Niño tests the resilience we have built; this one should also drive us to build more," it added.

articles.title: Major test for Australia's social media ban begins in High Court
articles.summary: Lawyers for Reddit and a digital rights group are arguing the world-leading policy robs children of their right to free communication.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Supplied: Digital Freedom Project Image caption, 
Australian teen Noah Jones is no longer a plaintiff in the case but will attend Tuesday's hearing By Lana Lam and Tiffanie Turnbull Sydney 
- Published 2 November 2026 Updated 3 November 2026 
Australia's rush to put in place a landmark social media ban for children led to "ill thought out" reforms which have robbed them of their right to free communication, the country's top court has been told. 
In a major test for the world-leading policy, online forum Reddit and a digital rights group argued at a hearing on Tuesday that the law should be struck down as it is unconstitutional. 
Introduced last December, the ban is among a number of online safety reforms the Australian government has spearheaded in recent years. 
Supporters say it protects children from harmful content, but critics say it is too blunt an instrument and efforts should focus on improving online safety. 
Speaking outside the High Court in Canberra, Communications Minister Anika Wells said the question of what society is willing to accept from tech platforms is "the most compelling policy question of our time". 
"We are here to defend a fundamental tenet of Australian democracy, which is an Australian's right, and particularly an Australian child's right, to be free from harm," Wells said. 
"We seek to defend that from sustained ideological attack." 
The constitutional challenge was filed by the Digital Freedom Project a few weeks before the ban started on 10 December last year. The group is led by New South Wales parliamentarian John Ruddick, who told reporters outside the court the policy amounted to "censorship". 
Two teens who originally spearheaded the case , Noah Jones and Macy Neyland, have since withdrawn as plaintiffs. The teens have yet to publicly state their reasons for doing so. 
But Jones told media outside the court that children deserved to have their voices heard. 
"If the children aren't collaborating and sharing their own views, then they're just spectators in their own world," he said, according to Nine newspapers. 
Reddit also launched a High Court challenge to the ban, arguing the policy has serious implications for privacy and political rights. 
The company said it shared Australia's goal of protecting young people online "but there are better and more effective ways" than a ban. 
"As we challenge this law in court, we'll continue to comply with it and advocate for more effective youth safety measures," said Reddit's chief communications officer Adam Collins. 
Inside the courtroom, the company's lawyer Perry Herzfeld argued the law breached the freedom of political expression implied in Australia's constitution by restricting children from the most important means of communication in the modern world. 
He said the ban was "ill thought out" and contradicted the advice of Australia's online safety tsar, and was rushed through without true public consultation - pointing out they had only 24 hours to make submissions about the law. 
Meanwhile government lawyer Joanna Davidson SC, began outlining for the full bench of the High Court why the government believed social media harmed children. She will continue presenting her case on Wednesday. 
Under the ban, ten platforms - Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, Snapchat, X, Kick, Threads and Twitch - must take "reasonable steps" to ensure no one under 16 years old can access its site. 
Platforms risk fines of up to A$99m (US$70m, £52m) for serious or repeated breaches, but since the ban started, no company has been fined. 
The eSafety Commissioner - the body tasked with enforcing the ban - has launched several investigations into alleged non-compliance by Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube. 
WhatsApp and online gaming sites like Roblox and Discord were not included in the ban, nor were educational platforms like YouTube Kids and Google Classroom. 
In the first few days of the ban, Meta - which owns three of the banned platforms - said it had closed about half a million accounts. 
Some children said they were booted off their accounts in the days before and when the ban started - but many have said they were able to easily circumvent the age checks which included uploading credit card details, photo IDs or a selfie.

articles.title: Wage protests force hundreds of Bangladesh garment factories to close
articles.summary: These factories, which manufacture for brands like H&M and Uniqlo, rely on millions of lowly paid workers.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Garment workers in Bangladesh stage protests to demand higher wages By Mukimul Ahsan ,  BBC Bangla   and   Koh Ewe 
- Published 3 November 2026 
Hundreds of garment factories in Bangladesh have been forced to close after days-long protests by workers demanding higher wages. 
On Sunday, protests in the capital Dhaka turned violent with protesters blocking roads, vandalising factories and setting vehicles on fire. They also clashed with police, who fired tear gas to disperse them. Police later said that dozens of protesters had been arrested. 
Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($242; £180), more than double the current standard, citing rising costs of living. 
Bangladesh's textile industry employs around four million workers and manufactures garments for major global brands including H&M, Primark and Uniqlo. 
There are fears in the industry that the prolonged unrest could disrupt production and affect international buyers, state news agency BSS reported. 
The garment industry generates nearly $40bn every year for Bangladesh, accounting for around 10% of its GDP. 
The South Asian nation is the world's second-largest garment exporter after China - but its workers are among the lowest-paid in the world, taking home around 13,000 taka ($105; £78) a month. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Protests turned violent with protesters blocking roads, vandalising factories and setting vehicles on fire 
"We want the government to accept our demands and increase our wages. [And] they need to instruct landlords and homeowners not to raise rent and ensure that the prices of essential commodities remain affordable," one female worker told BBC Bangla. 
"Food prices, cooking gas and electricity bills have all gone up," Mamun, a 28-year-old factory worker, told AFP. "The government must either bring down the prices of essential commodities or raise our wages." 
The government announced on Sunday that it had established a board to review workers' wages, and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman held an emergency meeting with ministers to address the unrest. 
But demonstrations continued on Monday in Dhaka and nearby manufacturing hubs including Ashulia, Gazipur and Narayanganj. 
Around 670 factories suspended operations on Monday, according to reports by Reuters and AFP, and hundreds in these areas will remain shut on Tuesday. 
At least 29 protesters were arrested as of Monday, according to Dhaka police Deputy Commissioner Mohidul Islam, who said that those who created an "unstable environment in the garment factories" would come under the law. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Garment workers demanding better wages clashed with police 
Authorities have accused the Awami League, the banned political party of former leader Sheikh Hasina, for taking advantage of the protest movement to instigate violence - though they did not provide any evidence of this. 
Home minister Salahuddin Ahmed threatened punitive action against protesters who were trying to "destabilise the country" "under the guise of labour protests". 
Babul Akhter, a workers' representative on the wage board, urged protesters to go back to work on Monday, promising to "fight for [their] fair wages". 
"I tell my fellow workers, return to work. Don't give in to anyone's incitement."

articles.title: Major tech stocks plunge as US midterms add to fears of AI slowdown
articles.summary: Markets have been reacting to possible tougher scrutiny of data centre construction and the AI industry following the US midterms.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images By Rachel Clun ,  Reporting from New York   and   Osmond Chia ,  Reporting from Singapore 
- Published 5 November 2026 Updated 17 minutes ago 
Hundreds of billions of dollars in market value has been wiped from major tech firms in the US and Asia in a stock market rout after the US midterm elections sparked concerns of a slowdown in artificial intelligence development. 
Shares in firms across the tech and AI sectors plummeted following Democratic wins after election campaigns run on slowing AI. 
The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite index closed down by more than 5.5%, losing an estimated $2.5tn (£1.9tn) in market value, according to Dow Jones data, while other key US stock indexes also saw big losses in their worst days since 2025. 
The sell-off comes on top of broader concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off. 
In Asia, tech-heavy indexes fell sharply on Friday morning as firms that make the computer chips and other equipment that power AI saw their shares slide. 
The Nikkei 225 in Japan was 6% lower in early trading as shares in memory chip maker Kioxia lost over 12.6% and rival Tokyo Electron slipped by 9.5%. 
South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix fell by more than 11.5%, while Samsung was down by nearly 10%. 
The sell-off in Seoul sent the Kospi index plunging more than 8.5%, triggering a so-called circuit breaker, a mechanism that temporarily halts trading to curb panic selling. 
Taiwan's Taiex dropped by more than 8.3%, with chipmaking giant TSMC falling by nearly 8.5%. 
It marks a "continuation of worries" over the level of spending on AI infrastructure, said MarketWatch chips analyst Britney Nguyen. 
Pressure on data centres 
Democrats in races across the US campaigned to slow the growth of data centres and AI, and there were dozens of measures on ballots around the country aimed at restricting the development of the hubs crucial for powering the technology. 
They won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of President Donald Trump's presidency. 
Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned heavily against data centres, pledging a moratorium on new construction in the sector. 
- 
Live: What can Democrats do with control of Congress? We answer your US midterms questions 
- 
Food, fuel and taxes – can the Democrats actually make life cheaper? 
- 
Boebert, billionaires' tax and other midterms races still to watch 
In a social media post, Trump blamed the slide on his political opponents. 
"The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election," he said. 
"Remember, it wasn't Republicans, it was Dumocrats. Do not fear, however, we will soon, one way or the other, be BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN!" 
Some Democrats have argued that AI has grown too big without any safeguards or oversight and have promised, with their new power in Congress, to change that. 
"Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future. NATIONAL DATA CENTER MORATORIUM NOW," Democrat Senator Bernie Sanders said in a post on X on Thursday. 
'Fresh panic' hits Wall Street 
Shares in companies heavily exposed to AI data centres, including crucial chipmakers and semiconductor manufacturers, fell sharply on Thursday, highlighting investor concerns that had already been growing. 
Nvidia shares slid more than 9%, knocking more than $400bn off the firm's market value. 
Other chipmakers also suffered, with AMD and Micron both dropping by more than 17%. Intel shares also dropped, down 10.3%, while memory card maker SanDisk plunged more than 22%. 
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which tracks the performance of 30 of the largest companies involved in semiconductor production, fell by more than 12%. 
Shares in Elon Musk's companies SpaceX and Tesla also plunged, falling 8% and nearly 11% respectively and shaving more than $300bn off the firms' market value on Thursday. 
Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas was turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday night. 
In total, the so-called magnificent seven tech companies, including Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, have shed a trillion dollars in value in a single trading day. 
The stock falls also hit other major US stock indexes. The S&P 500 index fell by 4.4% by the end of trading, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average erased gains made on Wednesday to close down more than 3.4%. 
The Nasdaq Composite fall was so large it is now in what market watchers call correction territory, which is where an index or company value falls at least 10% below its recent high. 
- 
A backlash over data centres is another threat to the AI juggernaut 
- Published 16 September 
- 
Big, noisy and coming to a town near you - why the data centre backlash is growing 
- Published 25 October 
Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said the steep sell-off on the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 was sending shockwaves into other markets. 
"Fresh panic over the AI trade has hit Wall Street hard," she said. 
"Fears that the vast sums poured into AI infrastructure may not deliver the returns investors have been banking on are now colliding with the prospect of a sharp slowdown in data centre construction." 
Greater scrutiny of data centre approvals, and their impact on the environment and electricity bills could delay projects and raise costs across the industry, said Charu Chanana, Chief Investment Strategist at Saxo. 
While both political parties are keen to ensure the US' dominance in the technology, "there is a difference between supporting AI development and allowing infrastructure to expand at any cost or pace," she said. 
Some tech leaders have said they were caught off guard by the backlash against data centres in the midterms. 
OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said he believed everyone had been surprised by the reaction to data centres, and more work needed to be done to ensure communities were on board. 
"A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can't just tweet and say: 'This is going to be good.' You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California on Wednesday evening. 
Meta's president Dina Powell McCormick said that the industry needed to put more effort into selling AI as a good idea. 
"I think we need to double and triple down on telling the story," she told the WSJ conference. 
Alongside the immediate impacts of the US mid-term elections, some investors have become concerned that AI shares could be in a bubble that is due a correction . 
With additional reporting from Lily Jamali

UK and US condemn ‘cruel’ second jail term handed to Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong
Foreign Office says 10-year sentence shows city’s security law is being used to ‘target individuals for political expression’ 
- 
Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison in national security case 
The UK and the US have condemned the 10-year sentence given to Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong under a controversial national security law. 
Wong, 30, was sentenced on Thursday after pleading guilty to “foreign collusion” under the law. He is the only person to have been prosecuted twice under the legislation that critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city. 
A spokesperson for the UK Foreign Office said that Wong’s sentence was “a clear example of how the National Security Law is being used to target individuals for political expression and participation”. 
The spokesperson added: “We call for an immediate end to all unjust prosecutions of individuals charged under the National Security Law and urge the authorities in China and Hong Kong to honour the rights and freedoms guaranteed to the people of Hong Kong under the Sino-British joint declaration (1984).” 
View image in fullscreen 
Pro-democracy umbrella movement protesters on the streets of Hong Kong in 2014. Photograph: Alex Hofford/EPA 
The US consulate in Hong Kong said in a statement that it “strongly condemns” the additional sentence and called for Wong’s immediate release. “Wong has been unjustly imprisoned since December 2020, demonstrating that Beijing will go to extraordinary lengths to silence those who advocate for fundamental freedoms in Hong Kong,” a consular spokesperson said. 
Shortly after the US consulate strongly condemned the sentence on Thursday, China warned “relevant parties” to “stop making irresponsible remarks” about Hong Kong judicial cases. 
Human rights groups and politicians from across the political spectrum also criticised the sentence. ‘I worry people will forget Hong Kong’: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison 
Read more 
Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch, said: “The harsh sentence on baseless charges against Joshua Wong is cruel and unjust. Young people promoting social change are an asset for any vibrant society, but the Hong Kong government puts them behind bars.” 
Sarah Brooks, deputy regional director for Amnesty International, said: “Today’s sentence is another grim reminder of how Hong Kong’s National Security Law has become a tool to punish dissent rather than to genuinely protect national security.” 
She said the new conviction “cruelly – and perhaps deliberately – comes mere months before he would have been eligible for release under his previous conviction”. 
Wong has already spent six years in detention and had been due for release in January 2027. 
In the most recent Foreign Office report on Hong Kong, published last month, the UK’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said that Wong’s case “reinforced concerns about the increasingly broad application of national security legislation”. 
Wong’s supporters called on governments around the world to push for his release. 
Nathan Law , a Hong Kong activist and friend of Wong’s who was named as a co-conspirator in the case, said: “It’s incredibly sad to see my friend Joshua Wong suffer another sentencing over his peaceful advocacy work for Hong Kong’s democracy.” 
Law called the sentencing “a farce” which signified that China “is determined to quash any hopes for freedom and democracy on its soil”. 
When former British colony Hong Kong was handed to China in 1997, it was promised 50 years of “one country two systems”, under which the city would keep some autonomy and freedoms. 
The UK considers Beijing to be in violation of that international treaty, after the crackdown on protests in 2019 and 2020, and the sweeping legal reforms that followed. 
Conservative MP Iain Duncan Smith said Wong had “stood up” for that treaty, which he said China had “subsequently trashed”. 
He added: “Despite this, the UK government has done little to nothing about it. The more we give in when China breaks the rules, the worse it gets in the future.” 
The Labour MP James Naish said: “Hongkongers in my constituency chose Britain for the freedoms Joshua is jailed for defending – values we should all support. This is not a lenient sentence and the government must show China that Britain will not tolerate it.”
